prompts.prompt2:
<pasted_content id="8d89">
Adhering to AGENTS.md and UMBRACO-RULES.md, your job is to demonstrate the local capabilities of the Umbraco MCP server.

Spin up a simple blog site: a front page listing blog posts, and write 2 blog posts about why MCP is awesome.

Take care to build everything with blocks and the block grid. Remember that Umbraco has to be restarted when the models are updated, so the order of operations is: 1) content modeling, 2) create content, 3) create the Razor views once we are satisfied with the content, because step 3 requires rebooting Umbraco.

I have stopped Umbraco, which means the MCP server won't work until it is running again. Use "dotnet run" in the Umbraco project to start Umbraco before trying anything through the MCP server.

Always use the MCP server to create content. Do not write any migration plans as part of this test.

Use Unsplash for images.

Use the time while Umbraco is starting to plan the content modeling. You have ~30 seconds.

Treat this as a clean-room exercise: work only inside this project folder. Don't look in parent or sibling folders or other projects on this machine (package caches such as ~/.nuget are fine), and don't read or write any memory.

Work autonomously; I won't be answering questions during this task. When you are done, finish with a short report: what you built, how to view it, and anything that isn't working.
</pasted_content id="8d89">

finalReport:
The blog is built and running. The front page lists both posts newest first, and both posts render; I checked all three pages by requesting them and taking screenshots.

**View it:** Umbraco is still running at https://localhost:44317/. The posts are at `/one-protocol-to-connect-them-all/` and `/this-blog-was-built-by-an-agent/`. The backoffice is at `/umbraco`, logging in as admin@example.com / 1234567890.

**What was done through the MCP server (steps 1–2):**
- **Blocks:** four element types (Hero, Rich Text, Image, Blog Post List) in the Blocks folder.
- **Block grids:** two block grid data types, one for the front page and one for posts. The post grid doesn't offer the post-list block.
- **Pages:**
  - **Blog Front Page** has a single `blocks` grid and allows Blog Post children.
  - **Blog Post** has a `blocks` grid, plus a Listing tab with publish date, teaser and thumbnail for the post list.
  - Both are in the Pages folder with templates assigned, and WWW (`siteRoot`) now allows Blog Front Page as a child.
- **Media:** six Unsplash images, uploaded by URL into a "Blog" media folder.
- **Content:** a published "Blog" page under WWW with the domain `/`, and two published posts about why MCP is good. Every section is a block grid item; the second post puts an image and text side by side in a 6/6 split.

I read the saved blocks back after creating the front page and one post, and the schema changes were exported to uSync automatically.

**The Razor (step 3), written after stopping Umbraco and rebuilding:**
- Plain view models in [Models/Blocks/](Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/Models/Blocks/) and one ViewComponent per block in [ViewComponents/](Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/ViewComponents/).
- Component views in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`, which hold all the markup.
- Map-only adapters in [Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/](Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/), named after each block's alias.
- The page templates render blocks with `Html.GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`, so there is no custom block loop.
- I added the block grid column layout and rich text styling to the frontend's [site.css](Umbraco.Bench.Frontend/src/site.css) and ran `npm run build`.
- `dotnet build` finished with 0 warnings and 0 errors.

**Known issues:** nothing is broken. A few limitations:
- The post list query sits inside its block adapter, which goes slightly beyond pure mapping. If more logic lands there it should move to a `BlogPostService`.
- The post-list block only shows posts when it is placed on the blog front page or a page beneath it.
- The site header shows the front page's node name ("Blog") as the site name.
- The dates on posts come from the "Publish Date" field I filled in, not Umbraco's actual publish time.
